proof.observed: Pre-fix, 100 runs: 39 EXITED WITHOUT DRAINING, each logging 'a second signal arrived while the broker was still starting up … it has served nothing' and exiting 1 on a process that had just answered a request. This head, 300 runs with the same harness: drained 300, exited without draining 0. The other half, which a careless fix would break — a second signal must END the drain, not merely fail to kill the process: 30 runs at BROKER_DRAIN_SECONDS=30, all 30 ended early with 'a second signal ended the drain early' and srv.Shutdown, slowest stop 0.03 s against a 30 s drain. A METHODOLOGY FINDING that matters for reading every earlier number here: two back-to-back SIGTERMs are merged by the kernel, since a non-realtime signal already pending is not queued, so a TERM-then-TERM harness often delivers one signal and never reaches the branch at all. It measured 10 of 300 (3.3%) where the same binary measures 39 of 100 (39%) once the two signals are SIGTERM and SIGINT — two different signals, which cannot merge, and both in the broker's own signal.Notify set. The reviewer's replica figure (2 of 300) and my first real-binary figure were both under-estimates for that reason, and the bias runs one way only.

And the 30-second-drain run above is the control against the other failure mode, a fix that makes the second signal unreachable: it would pass 300 of 300 while making every stop wait its whole drain out, and this head stops in 0.03 s.

proof.criterion: Reviewer finding 2, as the architect ruled it: the subscription must exist before the read whose result it is meant to invalidate, so a narrowing retag committed while a pod is loading is in force on that pod when it starts serving. A fix that merely shortens the gap does not pass however short it gets.
proof.surface: Two real cmd/broker processes on one Postgres, with the window HELD rather than raced for: pod B's BROKER_FAKE_SECRETS_FILE is a FIFO, so B sees only what the rig feeds it and each read blocks until a writer closes, which parks B inside its first policy load before any LISTEN exists. While B is parked the retag is committed to pod A's store and A is told to reread it, so A's notification goes out with no session of B's listening for it. B is then fed the pre-retag tags for every read of its first load and the post-retag tags from the moment its LISTEN is in place — the only read the catch-up load can make.

proof.negativeControl: The pre-fix build is the control and it fails the rig 5 of 5, so the rig discriminates rather than passing whatever it is given. My own earlier attempt at this rig did NOT discriminate and I record why, since it is a trap for the next person: a feeder that loops on `cat file > fifo` opens before a reader arrives, so the content is chosen early and whichever read comes next is served it — the catch-up read got the pre-retag tags however the switch was written, and the control read 0 as well. The feeder here opens the FIFO for writing (`exec 9>`), which blocks until a reader is actually there, and only then decides what to write, so there is exactly one content decision per read and it is taken with the reader already waiting.

notesForTheReviewer: Read the signal numbers with the merging in mind. A harness that sends SIGTERM twice back to back measures this defect at about a twelfth of its real rate, because the kernel does not queue a second pending SIGTERM. Any future measurement of a two-signal path here should use two different signals (SIGTERM then SIGINT, both in the broker's Notify set) or leave a gap, and should say which, because the two answers differ by more than an order of magnitude.

A gap changes what is being measured rather than only how reliably: with 100 ms between the signals the pre-fix build never exits either, because the watchdog's select finds `again` empty and takes the serveStarted arm. The defect needs both signals buffered before that select runs, which is what back-to-back delivery of two unmergeable signals gives. So the right harness for this branch is two different signals sent back to back.

The catch-up load leaves one residual, which limits.go states rather than hides: it reads the store's listing, so a store whose listing lags a write by up to its ListLag (five minutes on Secrets Manager, six hours on Secret Manager) can still show the pre-retag tags. The pod's `recent` anchors cover a name a reread settled, not one it never heard of, so this residual is real for exactly the case the catch-up is for. It is smaller than the five-minute reload it replaces and I record it rather than raise it.

The timeout arm of the bind's wait takes no catch-up, which the code says is deliberate: with no LISTEN there is no subscription to order a read after. That leaves a pod whose Postgres took the connection and never answered serving without the fan-out and without a catch-up, backstopped only by its five-minute reload — the same shape as a listener that is redialing, and documented in the same place.
